chapter: Ellington band members and life on the road
title: Finding food in segregated towns with Herb Jeffries and Sam Flaschnik
summary: On tour the band could not eat in many restaurants, so manager Sam Flaschnik, Jeffries and Bigard tricked a St. Louis cafe into cooking 26 meals, and Freddie Guy was told to use the back door even as a Creole.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Herb Jeffries told in an interview the other day, I understand, a radio interviewer, that when he was with Duke, you and he used to go to restaurants, on the road, to get the food in places, I guess, in the south where they wouldn't serve colored people, --
-- and so he said that was the main thing he did with the band, "Barney and I would go out and get the food or the band wouldn't have eaten." Is that right?

That's right. We came to St. Louis from a gig and so there wasn't a restaurant available to get something to eat. There was some, you know, but you couldn't go in there, see. So with the manager -- we had a little manager, Sam Flaschnik was his name -- and Herb and myself, whatever restaurant we'd see, we'd go up and we'd stop. So we saw this restaurant, there was nobody in it, the lights on. So Flaschnik said, "Watch, I'll fix that." He said, "Stop the bus back here and I'll go in front there." So he and Herb Jeffries and myself, we went into this restaurant and there's a guy coming out. It seemed as though he was so glad to see somebody in his place, see. So Sam said, "Can you serve 26 people right away?" So the guy says, "Depends on what they want." He said, "Well, ham and eggs, bacon and eggs." He says, "Oh, sure." He said, "I can fix it up as fast as you want it." He said, "Well, just fix up 26 right quick and I'll bring the people in because they're sitting out there." The guy says, "Sure." Sam says, "Now, when you're ready just holler."
So the guy, man, he fixed up those 26 plates and got it all fixed up, and Sam says, "Okay, fella,

bring them on in there. The stuff is ready." When they all walked in there and this guy saw it was nothing but coloons, he liked to have fainted. So Sam said, "What's the matter?" He said, "Uh, uh, nothing, nothing." But he wasn't going to throw that 26 -- those 26 plates away, though, you know. So we got to eating like that.

And so when we went into another place and just Sam and I went in there to get some sandwiches for the boys in the band, so Freddie Guy says, "Hell, if they can go in there, I can go in there too." So Freddie Guy walks in there. The guy says, "You have to go in the back." Freddie Guy says, "What do you mean I have to go in the back?" "Just what I said. If you want something to eat, you got to go in the back." He said, "Don't you know what I am?" The guy says, "You still got to go in the back." He says, "Man, I'm a Creole." The guy looked at him, he says, "I don't give a damn how old you is. You got to go in the back anyhow."
So we had -- Oh, then, we used to kid Freddie Guy.
Was that true in the south, or you meant in St. Louis, or was it true all over?
Oh, all over. Not all -- just the south on that place.
I mean, sometimes (unintelligible) true of other places besides the south?
